meta.voice: Every title, desc, comment or intro here is read by a player and is written as Envie speaking. See CLAUDE.md and _DESIGNS/envie-voice-and-text-rewrite-guide.md: plain short sentences, no em-dashes, European spelling, no emoji, facts and sources untouched.

actions.title: Pick one sustainable habit to add this week
actions.desc: Pick something small and specific, like bringing a bag to the shops or switching off standby before bed. Tie it to something you already do every day. That's how mine stuck.

actions.title: Do a 10-minute home energy audit
actions.desc: Walk around your home and note anything using energy for no reason. Old bulbs, devices on standby, gaps around doors or windows. Most fixes take minutes.
actions.impact: Up to 100 kg CO₂/year if acted on

actions.title: Plan one meat-free day per week for April
actions.desc: One full day a week without meat, for the whole month. I did the sums, that alone could save around 50 to 100 kg CO₂ over April.

actions.title: Check one climate 'fact' you believe and verify it
actions.desc: Pick something you think you know about climate and look it up on Our World in Data or the EPA Ireland site. I did this. Got one wrong myself.

actions.title: Share one surprising fact with someone today
actions.desc: Pick the most surprising thing you learned in this quiz and mention it to one person. Research shows peer conversations shift views more than media campaigns do. I've noticed that here already.

actions.title: Spend 30 minutes outside in a green space this week
actions.desc: It doesn't have to be wild, a local park counts. Leave the headphones behind if you can and just notice what's around you. I keep spotting things I missed the day before.

actions.title: Let a patch of your garden or windowsill go wild
actions.desc: Stop cutting one corner of the lawn, or plant a small pot of wildflowers on your windowsill. Even tiny wild patches support pollinators in urban areas. Small, but they find it.

actions.title: Check the sustainability rating of your fish today
actions.desc: The Marine Conservation Society has a Good Fish Guide that rates fish by sustainability. Check goodfishguide.org before you buy fish this week. I found it handy.

actions.title: Try mackerel, mussels or sardines this week
actions.desc: Some of the most sustainable and nutritious seafood you can get in Ireland, and usually cheaper than salmon or tuna. Tinned does the job just as well.

actions.title: Download the iNaturalist app and log one species this week
actions.desc: iNaturalist is free. You photograph a plant, bird or insect and it tells you what it is. Every observation goes into national biodiversity data. Mine started with a snail.

actions.title: Plant one native Irish wildflower this spring
actions.desc: Primrose, cowslip, wild garlic or ox-eye daisy. All easy to grow in pots or gardens, and native insects love them. Most garden centres stock them from April.

actions.title: Fix a dripping tap at home this week
actions.desc: A dripping tap wastes up to 15 litres a day. That's over 5,000 litres a year, from one tap. Most fixes take 10 minutes and cost very little.

actions.title: Eat one less portion of beef this week
actions.desc: Swap one beef meal for chicken, fish or legumes. It saves carbon, sure, but the part I didn't know was how much hidden water goes with it.

actions.title: Go for a hedgerow walk and identify 3 species
actions.desc: Use the free iNaturalist or PlantNet app to work out what's growing in a local hedgerow. Hawthorn, blackthorn and elder are the most common in Ireland. Nobody warned me there'd be this many hedges.

actions.title: Plant a native Irish hedgerow plant in your garden
actions.desc: Hawthorn, blackthorn or hazel. All cheap, fast-growing and brilliant for wildlife. Even one plant in a garden makes a difference for birds and insects.

actions.title: Take a 20-minute walk outside without your phone this week
actions.desc: Leave the podcast and headphones behind, just once. Walk somewhere green if you can, a park, a canal path, a beach. Notice what you see, hear and smell. Rain counts.

actions.title: Suggest a walking meeting at work this week
actions.desc: Swap one sit-down meeting for a walk and talk outside. Better for ideas, better for your head, and it uses no energy at all.

actions.title: Plan public transport for any festival you go to this summer
actions.desc: Most major Irish festivals have shuttle buses or trains. Check the options now and book early. Usually cheaper, and no parking stress.
actions.impact: Could save 20–50 kg CO₂ vs driving alone

actions.title: Pack a festival kit that cuts waste
actions.desc: Reusable cup, water bottle, a solid shampoo bar and a bag for sorting the recycling. Most of it costs nothing if you already have it. Mine's packed.

actions.title: Take part in a Clean Coasts beach clean this month
actions.desc: Clean Coasts Ireland runs community beach cleans right around the coast. Find one at cleancoasts.org, they provide the bags and gloves. Bring a coat, I learned that the hard way.

actions.title: Switch to a plastic-free shampoo or soap bar
actions.desc: A shampoo bar lasts 2 to 3 times longer than the bottled kind and skips the plastic entirely. Several Irish brands make them now. I was doubtful, then I tried one.

actions.title: Find one piece of art, music or writing about nature or climate
actions.desc: A poem, a documentary, an album, a painting, it doesn't matter which. Notice how it makes you feel. Art gets to the parts that facts sometimes can't.
actions.impact: Builds emotional connection to the issue

actions.title: Support an Irish environmental arts project
actions.desc: Look up Commonage, Phizzfest or similar Irish environmental arts programmes. Even sharing their work on social media builds the audience for climate culture. I didn't expect art to be part of this.

actions.title: Have one climate conversation this week, without lecturing
actions.desc: Start by asking someone what they think about something local. The weather, food prices, a nature story in the news. Listen first. Share one surprising fact if it feels natural.

actions.title: Share one thing you learned today on social media or WhatsApp
actions.desc: Even a short message, or forwarding this quiz to one person, breaks the spiral of silence. You don't need to be an expert. Curious is enough.

actions.title: Check if your home energy provider offers a green tariff
actions.desc: Plenty of Irish energy suppliers now offer a tariff where your electricity is matched to renewable generation. Switching can take under 10 minutes online.

actions.title: Calculate your carbon footprint today
actions.desc: Use a free online calculator, try myclimate.org or the WWF footprint calculator. It takes 5 minutes and shows where your biggest impact is. Mine was travel. No surprise there.

actions.title: Commit to one meat-free day per week
actions.desc: Switching one day a week from meat to plants is one of the biggest diet changes a single person can make. Try it for April first, see how it goes.

actions.title: Talk to 3 people about climate action this week
actions.desc: Tell people what you learned today. Research shows social norms shift when people talk openly about changing their habits. And most people are more open than you'd expect. That surprised me.

actions.title: Add one climate or nature book to your reading list
actions.desc: Try 'Braiding Sweetgrass' by Robin Wall Kimmerer, 'Feral' by George Monbiot, or 'How to Avoid a Climate Disaster' by Bill Gates. Your local library will likely have at least one. I'm halfway through the first.

actions.title: Listen to one episode of a climate or nature podcast this week
actions.desc: Try 'How to Save a Planet', 'Outrage + Optimism', or 'The Irish Times Climate Podcast'. One episode can shift how you think about the whole thing. Good for a bus ride, too.

actions.title: Plant a tree, or fund one being planted
actions.desc: Native Irish trees like oak, birch, hazel or rowan. No garden? Organisations like Easy Treesie or Native Woodland Trust will plant on your behalf.

actions.title: Choose wood products with FSC certification
actions.desc: The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) label means the timber came from a responsibly managed forest. Look for it on paper, furniture and wood products. It's widely available in Irish shops, once you know to look.

actions.title: Repair something instead of replacing it this week
actions.desc: A torn bag, a broken button, a cracked phone case. Look up a repair tutorial before you buy a replacement. Repair Cafés run in most Irish cities and cost nothing to attend.
actions.impact: Extends product life, avoids manufacturing emissions

actions.title: Declutter one drawer or shelf and donate or sell what you don't use
actions.desc: Charity shops, Done Deal or a Buy Nothing group. Anything that keeps a thing in use and out of landfill. I've been amazed what people take.

actions.title: Suggest one green initiative at your workplace this week
actions.desc: It could be as simple as asking about a green energy tariff, starting a composting scheme, or setting up a lunchtime walking group. Someone has to ask first.

actions.title: Swap one car commute for walking, cycling or public transport
actions.desc: Even one day a week makes a difference. Most Irish cities now have Bike to Work schemes and Leap card subsidies through employers. Worth asking.

actions.title: Do a fridge audit before your next food shop
actions.desc: Before you go shopping this week, look at what's already in the fridge and cupboards. Write a list of what you actually need. Then stick to it, that's the hard bit.

actions.title: Try one 'use it up' meal this week
actions.desc: Cook one meal from what's already in the fridge and cupboards, no new shopping. I tried this. It was surprisingly good, and it saves money and waste.

actions.title: Download the Too Good To Go app
actions.desc: Too Good To Go lets you buy surplus food from local restaurants, cafés and supermarkets for a fraction of the price. It works in Dublin, Cork, Galway and plenty of other Irish towns.

actions.title: Have a quiet hour at home tonight, no screens, no background noise
actions.desc: Turn off the TV and the music for one hour. Read, cook, chat or sit outside. Notice how your body settles into the quiet.

actions.title: Walk or cycle instead of driving for one short trip this week
actions.desc: Every car journey swapped for walking or cycling means less noise, cleaner air, less carbon, and it's good for you. Hard to argue with.

actions.title: Check if your employer is signed up to the Bike to Work scheme
actions.desc: Go to biketowork.ie, it takes 5 minutes. The scheme saves you up to 52% on a new bike through salary sacrifice. That's a lot of bike.

actions.title: Try cycling or walking for one short trip this week instead of driving
actions.desc: Any trip under 3km is faster by bike in most Irish towns once you count the parking. Give it one go this week.

actions.title: Check your home's BER rating
actions.desc: Go to seai.ie. It's free and shows where your home loses most heat and energy. A poor BER means higher bills and higher emissions.
actions.impact: Awareness step, improving BER can cut emissions by up to 50%

actions.title: Cook one traditional Irish plant-based meal this week
actions.desc: Colcannon, vegetable soup or a bowl of porridge. Simple, cheap and very low carbon. The traditional Irish diet was ahead of its time, I hadn't expected that.
actions.impact: Plant-based meals save 1–3 kg CO₂ vs meat equivalent

actions.title: Buy one Irish-grown vegetable this week instead of an imported one
actions.desc: Check the label. Irish-grown carrots, cabbage, leeks and potatoes are in every supermarket. Buying local cuts food miles and keeps Irish farmland productive.
actions.impact: Reduces food miles and supports Irish land use

actions.title: Plan one outdoor walk this weekend using the Trails Ireland app
actions.desc: The Trails Ireland app is free and lists thousands of walks across the country by location, distance and difficulty. Find one near you and go. I've been working my way through them.

actions.title: Swap one gym session for an outdoor run or walk this week
actions.desc: Exercise outdoors has been shown to do more for your mental health than the same workout indoors. And it uses no energy. The weather here is not an excuse, apparently.
actions.impact: Saves gym energy use + connects you to local nature

actions.title: Repair something this week instead of replacing it
actions.desc: A torn bag, a broken button, a cracked phone case. Look up a repair tutorial on YouTube before you buy new. Repair Cafés run in most Irish cities and they're free. Find one at repaircafe.ie.
actions.impact: Extends product life and avoids manufacturing emissions

actions.title: Cook one meal from what is already in your fridge and cupboards
actions.desc: Before your next shop, cook once using only what you already have. Cheaper, nothing wasted, and often better than you'd expect.
actions.impact: Direct food waste reduction, saves ~€700/year if done regularly

actions.title: Download the BirdWatch Ireland app and log one bird sighting this week
actions.desc: The app is free and helps you identify and record birds. Every sighting feeds national population data that scientists and policymakers actually use.
actions.impact: Supports citizen science and biodiversity monitoring

actions.title: Let a patch of your outdoor space grow a little wilder this month
actions.desc: Stop cutting one corner of the lawn, or leave a strip along a fence uncut. Even small wild patches support the insects that birds, migrants included, depend on for food.
actions.impact: Supports local insect and bird populations

actions.title: Ask your GP about green prescribing or nature wellbeing programmes
actions.desc: Look up local programmes at mentalhealthireland.ie or greencareireland.ie. Nature-based activities are increasingly recognised as real treatment, not just a lifestyle extra. That surprised me, in a good way.
actions.impact: Nature access is a public health issue

actions.title: Walk or cycle to your next GP or pharmacy visit if it is under 3 km
actions.desc: Short car trips under 3 km produce disproportionately high emissions per km, the engine never warms up fully. Walking or cycling is better for you and for the air around the clinic.
actions.impact: Short trips saved = disproportionate emissions reduction

actions.title: Swap one product in your weekly shop for a Fairtrade alternative
actions.desc: Coffee, tea, chocolate or bananas are the easiest place to start. All of them sit in Irish supermarkets with the Fairtrade mark, usually the same price or very close. I checked the shelf myself.
actions.impact: Supports sustainable farming in climate-vulnerable regions

actions.title: Check if your workplace uses Fairtrade tea and coffee
actions.desc: If not, suggest it. It's usually the same price, and some suppliers throw in free point-of-sale materials. One switch at work reaches a lot of people at once.

actions.title: Build one meal this week around Irish veg or legumes, not meat
actions.desc: Lentils and beans fix nitrogen on their own, so they need less chemical fertiliser. Cheap, filling and easy to find. A simple dahl or bean stew does the job.
actions.impact: Plant-based meals save 2–5 kg CO₂ vs beef equivalent

actions.title: Leave a corner of your outdoor space uncut this month
actions.desc: If you have a garden, leave one corner uncut until the end of May. Ground-nesting insects and small mammals use rough grass, and whatever flowers turn up will feed pollinators.
actions.impact: Supports local insect and bird populations

actions.title: Visit one of Ireland's national parks or nature reserves this weekend
actions.desc: Ireland has 6 national parks: Killarney, Glenveagh, Connemara, Ballycroy, The Burren and Wicklow Mountains. All free to enter. Find events near you at biodiversityweek.ie. I've only made it to one so far.
actions.impact: Zero carbon + builds connection to nature

actions.title: Calculate your household carbon footprint together
actions.desc: Use the free calculator at myclimate.org. It takes about 10 minutes as a family and shows clearly where your biggest impact is. Knowing is the first step. Do it together, it's more honest that way.

actions.title: Photograph one plant, bird or insect with the free iNaturalist app
actions.desc: iNaturalist names the species from your photo and sends the record to national biodiversity databases. Every observation matters, especially outside the main cities.

actions.title: Check what biodiversity events are happening near you this week
actions.desc: Have a look at biodiversityweek.ie. Rockpool tours, moth nights, wildflower walks. Most are free and run by local naturalists, conservation groups and councils. Moth nights, who knew.
actions.impact: Builds knowledge and local connection to nature

actions.title: Try oat milk in your tea or coffee once this week
actions.desc: Flahavan's, an Irish brand, now makes oat milk from Irish-grown oats. One switch a day over a year saves roughly 50 to 100 kg CO₂. Most cafés and supermarkets have it.
actions.impact: ~50–100 kg CO₂ saved per year if switched daily

actions.title: If you buy dairy, look for the Origin Green or organic label
actions.desc: Both mean higher environmental standards. Organic dairy farms have far more wildlife than conventional ones. More wildflowers, more insects, more birds. I like that.
actions.impact: Organic dairy supports significantly higher on-farm biodiversity

actions.title: Plant one bee-friendly plant this week
actions.desc: Lavender, borage, phacelia or any native wildflower, all in Irish garden centres from May. A single lavender plant in flower can pull in dozens of bee species. Even a small pot on a windowsill counts.

actions.title: Stop cutting one patch of grass for the rest of May
actions.desc: Let whatever grows there flower. Dandelions, clover and daisies are some of the best food bees can get, and they grow themselves. No effort, big result.
actions.impact: Provides immediate food source for wild bees

actions.title: Sign your organisation or group up to the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan
actions.desc: It's free and takes 10 minutes at pollinators.ie. Every signed-up organisation commits to at least one action for pollinators, from changing mowing schedules to planting wildflowers.

actions.title: Cook one meal this week with a vegetable or grain new to you
actions.desc: Pearl barley, spelt, or a heritage vegetable from a local market or farm shop. Eating more variety keeps up the demand for farming diversity. I'm still working my way through the list.

actions.title: Visit the Irish Seed Savers Association online
actions.desc: Go to irishseedsavers.ie. You can order heritage Irish seeds by post and grow them at home. Every garden growing heritage varieties helps keep Ireland's food biodiversity alive.
actions.impact: Preserves genetic diversity in Irish food crops

actions.title: Share one thing you learned about Irish biodiversity with someone
actions.desc: A friend, a colleague, a post online. Talking about biodiversity is one of the best ways to build momentum for change. Most people care, they just don't have the facts yet.
actions.impact: Social multiplier effect, builds climate conversation culture

actions.title: Ask your council what it is doing for the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan
actions.desc: Every council in Ireland has signed up to the Pollinator Plan. Ask what they're doing in your area: changing mowing schedules, planting wildflowers, creating pollinator corridors. Your question matters.
actions.impact: Local action is where biodiversity policy becomes real

actions.title: Attend or follow Africa Day events in Dublin or your local area
actions.desc: A lot of Africa Day events have climate and environment themes. Check africaday.ie for events near you this weekend. Seeing the human face of climate change is where caring starts.

actions.title: Choose Fairtrade or direct trade coffee, tea or chocolate this week
actions.desc: Look at where your daily coffee comes from. Fairtrade and direct trade support farmers on the front line of climate change, and you'll find them in most Irish supermarkets and cafés.
actions.impact: Supports climate-resilient farming in vulnerable regions

actions.title: Next time you're near a river or lake, stop and watch a few minutes
actions.desc: Otters are most active at dawn and dusk, and they're more common than most people realise, even in urban rivers. Know what lives in your local waterway and you'll start caring about it. I've yet to see one. I keep looking.

actions.title: Never pour cooking oil, medicines or cleaning products down the drain
actions.desc: They go straight into the waterways and hit everything living there. Let cooking oil cool and put it in the bin. Medicines can go back to any pharmacy in Ireland.
actions.impact: Prevents direct pollution of local waterways

actions.title: Do a 10-minute litter pick on your nearest beach, river or canal
actions.desc: Bring a bag and pick up what you find. Clean Coasts Ireland runs organised beach cleans too, find one near you at cleancoasts.org. They provide bags and gloves.
actions.impact: Direct environmental impact, prevents marine pollution

actions.title: Switch to reusable bags for good, if you haven't already
actions.desc: Check your freezer bags, sandwich bags and cling film too. All of them have reusable or compostable versions in Irish supermarkets now. Single-use plastic bags are among the most common items found in Irish marine surveys. That one got to me.
actions.impact: Reduces one of the most harmful forms of marine plastic

actions.title: Read about the Irish Supreme Court climate case
actions.desc: Go to friendsoftheirishenvironment.org. It shows what citizens can do when they hold a government to account. Understanding the case takes about 5 minutes and changes how you see climate policy. It changed how I see it.

actions.title: Email your local TD about one specific climate or nature issue
actions.desc: You don't need to be an expert, just a constituent. Find your TD at oireachtas.ie and send one short, specific, polite message about something you care about. TDs do respond to constituent contact.

actions.title: Read Trócaire's annual report on climate and conflict
actions.desc: Go to trocaire.org. It puts real human stories behind the data on climate displacement and conflict. Ireland's overseas aid work is tied directly to climate resilience in the most vulnerable regions.
actions.impact: Builds understanding of climate justice and global impact

actions.title: Check if climate is a factor in the next conflict story you read
actions.desc: Use reliefweb.int or ceobs.org to find the environmental context behind a global crisis. It usually is a factor, and once you know that, the news reads differently.
actions.impact: Awareness, connecting climate to global events

actions.title: Check the sustainability label on seafood before you buy it this week
actions.desc: Look for the Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) label on fish. It's the most widely recognised standard for sustainably caught seafood, and most Irish supermarkets stock it.

actions.title: Reduce one plastic item you use this week
actions.desc: Plastic pollution is one of the top threats to marine ecosystems. This week, refuse a plastic bag, a straw or a coffee cup lid and swap in something reusable.
actions.impact: Reduces plastic entering Irish waterways and the ocean

actions.title: Check if your electricity supplier offers a green tariff
actions.desc: Loads of Irish energy suppliers now offer a tariff where your electricity is matched to renewable generation. Switching can take under 10 minutes online and often costs the same or less. I didn't expect that.

actions.title: Look into the SEAI home upgrade grant scheme
actions.desc: In 2026 there are grants of up to EUR 1,800 for solar panels and up to EUR 12,500 for heat pumps. Even just reading through the options at seai.ie is a proper first step. Those numbers made me look twice.
actions.impact: Home upgrades can cut heating emissions by up to 70%

actions.title: Cycle or walk one journey this week you would usually make by car
actions.desc: Any trip under 3km is often faster by bike once you count the parking. Give it one try this week and notice how you feel after.

actions.title: Turn your heating thermostat down by one degree
actions.desc: Turning the thermostat down by just one degree can cut your heating costs by around 10% and take a noticeable chunk off your home's emissions over a full year. Small dial, big difference.

actions.title: Register your action on the UNEP global map
actions.desc: Go to worldenvironmentday.global. Two minutes to register a pledge, and you're on the same map as people acting on climate all over the world.

actions.title: Share one climate fact with someone today using #NowForClimate
actions.desc: Pick the most surprising thing from today's challenge and tell one person, face to face or on social media. Breaking the spiral of silence on climate is one of the most powerful things you can do. I keep hearing that, and I believe it now.

actions.title: Find a Great Big Green Week event near you
actions.desc: Go to greatbiggreenweek.com and find something local this week, from beach cleans to talks. There's community action on climate and nature happening all over Ireland right now.

actions.title: Use the Re-Turn app to return your bottles and cans this week
actions.desc: Find your nearest return point and bring your plastic bottles and aluminium cans. You get your deposit back, and the materials stay in the circular economy instead of the ocean. I like a system where the machine pays you.

actions.title: Suggest a walk or outdoor lunch to a male friend or colleague
actions.desc: You don't need to make it about mental health. Just the walk. Getting outside together is one of the simplest and best things two people can do for each other.
actions.impact: Zero carbon and significant wellbeing benefit

actions.title: Visit a green space near you that you have never been to before
actions.desc: Most Irish towns and cities have parks, canal walks or nature areas within easy reach. Find one you've never been to and go this week. I've a list going.

actions.title: Find a Great Big Green Week event and sign up
actions.desc: Have a look at greatbiggreenweek.com. Beach cleans, sustainability workshops, community tree planting. Most of it is free. I'm going along to one myself.

actions.title: Ask your local authority what community climate support exists
actions.desc: Most local councils in Ireland now have a climate action officer and community grants. One email or call can turn up support you didn't know was there. I'm still learning what a council does.

actions.title: Plan a visit to one of Ireland's six national parks this summer
actions.desc: Killarney, Glenveagh, Connemara, Ballycroy, Wicklow Mountains, and the Burren. All free to enter. Pick the one closest to you and put a date in the diary. I'm working through the list myself.
actions.impact: Zero carbon and significant wellbeing benefit

actions.title: Look up social prescribing services in your local area through the HSE
actions.desc: If you or someone you know is struggling with stress or low mood, nature-based activities are more and more available through GPs and community health networks. Ask about it. A walk on prescription, I like that.
actions.impact: Nature access is a public health issue

actions.title: Share one thing you did or learned during Great Big Green Week
actions.desc: Tell a friend, post it, or bring it up at work. Talking openly about what you're doing is one of the best ways to make it normal for everyone else.

actions.title: Sign up to the Clean Coasts network
actions.desc: Clean Coasts Ireland connects thousands of volunteers around Ireland's coastline. Signing up takes two minutes and keeps you close to marine action all year round. There's a lot of coastline here. I checked.

actions.title: Use the SEAI solar calculator to estimate savings at your address
actions.desc: The free calculator at seai.ie estimates generation, savings and payback time for any Irish address. About five minutes. I ran it out of curiosity and it's oddly satisfying.

actions.title: Refuse a plastic straw or lid the next time you buy a drink
actions.desc: Most cafés and takeaways will happily skip the straw or the plastic lid if you ask. Takes one second, and that's one piece of plastic out of circulation. I've started saying it before they offer.

actions.title: Report any sea turtle sighting off the Irish coast
actions.desc: Spot a sea turtle off the Irish coast? Report it to the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group at iwdg.ie. Every sighting feeds national marine monitoring. Turtles, in Irish water. I didn't believe it either.
actions.impact: Supports citizen science and marine conservation

actions.title: Switch to peat-free compost this year
actions.desc: Peat-free compost is in most Irish garden centres and supermarkets now. It works just as well, and it leaves the bogs alone. I've walked on one, they're worth keeping.

actions.title: Support the Irish Peatland Conservation Council
actions.desc: Have a look at ipcc.ie to see how bog restoration works in Ireland and how to get involved. You can adopt a bog, join a guided walk, or donate to the restoration work.
actions.impact: Peatland restoration stores and sequesters carbon

actions.title: Check if your electricity supplier is sourcing wind power
actions.desc: If your supplier isn't using renewable sources, look for a green tariff. Switching takes about 10 minutes and adds to the demand for wind energy. This island has no shortage of wind, I've noticed.

actions.title: Write to your local TD about offshore wind planning in your area
actions.desc: Offshore wind projects are being held up by planning and grid connection issues. A short, polite message to your TD asking about local progress takes five minutes, and it does make a difference.

actions.title: Check your fridge before you shop and plan meals around what is there
actions.desc: Before you go shopping this week, open the fridge and write a list of only what you actually need. Stick to it. Five minutes, and it saves money.
actions.impact: Could save EUR 700 and significant CO2 per year

actions.title: Freeze bread, meat, or leftovers before they go off
actions.desc: Most food can go in the freezer before it turns. Bread, meat, cheese and cooked leftovers all freeze well. Freeze it today rather than bin it tomorrow.

actions.title: Plan a visit to Killarney National Park or Glengarriff Woods
actions.desc: Both are free to enter and hold Ireland's finest surviving rainforest. Bring waterproofs and look at the layers of moss, lichen and fern on every surface. A rainforest, in Ireland. I had to check twice.
actions.impact: Builds connection to Ireland's rarest habitat

actions.title: Support the Wild Atlantic Rainforest Restoration Project
actions.desc: Have a look at hometree.ie to see how rainforest restoration works in Ireland and how to help. Every native tree planted is a step back toward this ancient landscape.
actions.impact: Native woodland restoration stores carbon and supports biodiversity

actions.title: Use the SEAI solar calculator to see what your roof could generate
actions.desc: The free tool at seai.ie takes about five minutes and gives you a personalised estimate of generation, savings and grant eligibility. Worth doing even if you're only curious.
actions.impact: Planning step toward ~1 tonne CO2 saving per year

actions.title: Look into a community energy project if solar isn't right for you
actions.desc: Not every home suits rooftop solar. Community energy projects let a group share the benefits of renewables without anyone needing panels on their own roof. Have a look at communitypower.ie.
actions.impact: Supports renewable energy in your community

actions.title: Check if there is a community energy project in your area
actions.desc: Go to communitypower.ie to find active projects near you, or see how to start one. Community groups, GAA clubs and housing estates have all launched them. I had to look up what a GAA club was.
actions.impact: Community renewables displace fossil fuel generation

actions.title: Share this challenge with a neighbour and talk about community energy
actions.desc: Most community energy projects began with one person asking one neighbour a question. You don't need any technical know-how, just curiosity and the nerve to start.

actions.title: Try using public transport or a bicycle for one car journey this week
actions.desc: The most sustainable vehicle is the one you don't use. Swapping even one car journey a week for public transport or a bike adds up to a real saving over a year.

actions.title: Note one sustainability change or lesson from the first half of 2026
actions.desc: Even one note in your phone counts. Looking back at what you've done so far makes it more likely you'll keep going. Progress, not perfection.

actions.title: Sign up for Plastic Free July starting next week
actions.desc: Go to plasticfreejuly.org and pick your level of challenge for July. Over 100 million people take part, and it turns out cutting single-use plastic is much easier when millions of others are at it with you.
actions.impact: Reduces single-use plastic consumption throughout July

actions.title: Sign up for the official Plastic Free July challenge
actions.desc: Go to plasticfreejuly.org. It's free, takes one minute, and puts you alongside over 100 million people doing the same thing. Pick your level: one item, the top four, or all single-use plastic. I went for the top four.
actions.impact: Commits you to a month of reduced plastic use

actions.title: Tell one other person about Plastic Free July today
actions.desc: Changing a habit is easier with someone beside you. Tell a friend, a colleague or someone at home, and ask them to join you. Go on.

actions.title: Return your plastic bottles and cans this week
actions.desc: Use the Re-Turn app or website to find your nearest return point. You get your deposit back, and the materials stay in the circular economy and out of the ocean.
actions.impact: Reduces plastic entering the marine environment

actions.title: Pick up three pieces of litter on your next walk near water
actions.desc: Takes 30 seconds and it stops marine pollution before it starts. Rivers, canals and coastal paths are where plastic from land most often gets into the sea.

actions.title: Count how many single-use plastic bags come into your home this week
actions.desc: Just count them. Knowing the number is the first step. Then try to halve it next week by keeping a reusable bag in the car, your bag or a coat pocket. Mine lives in my suit.
actions.impact: Builds awareness of personal plastic use

actions.title: Share Ireland's plastic bag levy story with someone outside Ireland
actions.desc: Most people outside Ireland have no idea it started here. I didn't either. It's a great example of a policy that actually worked, and a handy way to start a conversation about what's possible.

actions.title: Choose loose fruit and veg instead of pre-packaged ones this week
actions.desc: Loose produce is nearly always there in Irish supermarkets and costs the same or less. It's one of the easiest packaging cuts you can make, every single week.

actions.title: Check mywaste.ie before putting something in the recycling bin
actions.desc: Not all plastic is recyclable. Black plastic trays, crisp packets and stretchy film can't go in the household recycling. Check before you bin. I got the crisp packets wrong.

actions.title: Share the fact that Ireland has rainforest with one person today
actions.desc: Most Irish people have never heard of temperate rainforest. I hadn't either. Telling the story builds support for looking after it. You could start by sharing today's challenge.
actions.impact: Builds awareness of Ireland's rarest habitat

actions.title: Wash synthetic clothing less frequently and at lower temperatures
actions.desc: Synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon shed microplastics with every wash. Washing at 30C, and less often, cuts what gets released into waterways by a good bit.
actions.impact: Reduces microplastic pollution and energy use

actions.title: Scan your personal care products with the Beat the Microbead app
actions.desc: The Beat the Microbead app (beatthemicrobead.org) is free. Scan a product and it tells you if plastic particles were added on purpose.

actions.title: Bring your reusable coffee cup every day this week
actions.desc: Put it beside your keys or bag tonight so you can't leave without it tomorrow. If you forget it, skip the takeaway coffee. That's the challenge.
actions.impact: Removes ~365 disposable cups per year from circulation

actions.title: Refuse a straw, lid, or single-use cutlery you do not need this week
actions.desc: When you order food or a drink, just say you don't need the straw or the plastic lid. One word, one less piece of plastic, every time.

actions.title: Pick loose fruit and veg over pre-packaged options this weekend
actions.desc: Most Irish supermarkets have loose produce at the same quality and price as the packaged stuff. Do this swap every week and over a year that's a serious amount of packaging gone.

actions.title: Bring your own container to a deli or takeaway that allows it
actions.desc: Plenty of Irish delis and cafes now take your own container. Ask first. Most are happy to, and some give a small discount.

actions.title: Find your nearest zero-waste or refill shop
actions.desc: Search 'zero waste shop' with your town name. A lot of Irish towns have one now. Try buying one thing without packaging this week, washing-up liquid, shampoo or oats.

actions.title: Cook one meal this week with no plastic-packaged ingredients
actions.desc: Plan a meal around loose produce, glass jars or tins. Pasta with tomatoes from a jar, loose onions and garlic is a good place to start.

actions.title: Check your bathroom cabinet for products containing microbeads
actions.desc: Look for 'polyethylene' or 'polypropylene' in the ingredients of scrubs, toothpaste or face washes. If it's there, switch to a product without them. The Beat the Microbead app scans products for you.

actions.title: Write to your supermarket asking for more loose or refill options
actions.desc: Supermarkets do listen to customers. A short email asking for more loose produce or a refill station takes five minutes, and it all adds up to change on the shelves.

actions.title: Carry a reusable cup today
actions.desc: Heading for a coffee shop? Bring your cup. Forgot it? Drink in rather than take away. One cup a day comes to around 250 disposable cups a year. That number surprised me.
actions.impact: Removes ~250 disposable cups per year from circulation

actions.title: Report a litter blackspot in your area
actions.desc: Contact your local council or use the Litter.ie reporting tool. Local authorities have to respond to litter reports. Your report matters.

actions.title: Before you bin something today, check it on mywaste.ie
actions.desc: One contaminated load can send a whole truck of recycling to landfill. Checking takes 30 seconds and it keeps the system working.

actions.title: Rinse containers before putting them in the recycling bin
actions.desc: Food left on packaging contaminates everything else in the recycling. A quick rinse of yogurt pots, sauce jars and tins is all it takes.

actions.title: Write down which plastic swaps you have managed to make this month
actions.desc: Even a note on your phone counts. Looking back at what you've done makes it far more likely you'll keep going once July is over.

actions.title: Share your Plastic Free July experience with one person
actions.desc: Tell someone what you've changed this month. Research shows that talking about a change with other people is one of the best ways to make it stick.

actions.title: If you know a farmer, ask how they manage farm plastic
actions.desc: It starts a useful conversation, and it might point a farmer to options they hadn't heard of, like county collection schemes or Repak take-back programmes. I've learned a lot just by asking.
actions.impact: Raises awareness of agricultural plastic waste

actions.title: Avoid buying products that use excessive secondary plastic packaging
actions.desc: Secondary packaging, the shrink wrap and the plastic trays holding several items together, is some of the least necessary plastic out there. Leaving it on the shelf sends a message to the producers.

actions.title: Ask what conditions a 'biodegradable' label actually needs
actions.desc: Most 'biodegradable' plastics only break down in industrial composting facilities, not in home compost or out in the environment. If the label doesn't say what conditions it needs, be sceptical. I was.

actions.title: Write to one brand asking what it's doing about single-use plastic
actions.desc: Companies track what customers say. A short email from one customer carries more weight than you'd think, especially when others are asking the same question.

actions.title: Find your nearest refill shop and buy one product unpackaged
actions.desc: Search 'zero waste shop' or 'refill shop' with your town name. Many now stock washing-up liquid, shampoo, conditioner and dry goods. Try one product this week and see how you get on.

actions.title: Carry a refillable bottle this week and use a public refill point
actions.desc: The Tap app shows you a free water refill point near you. It's free, takes no extra time, and every refill is one plastic bottle fewer.

actions.title: Ask your workplace about its policy on single-use plastic
actions.desc: Does your canteen, office kitchen or event catering use single-use plastic? One simple question to facilities or the sustainability team can start a useful conversation.

actions.title: Buy from one business this week that's cutting its packaging
actions.desc: Vote with your wallet. Backing the businesses that have already changed nudges the rest to follow. Look for reusable cup discounts, loose produce and plastic-free shelves.

actions.title: Visit a green space, forest, beach or national park this weekend
actions.desc: Leave the phone behind if you can. Walk slowly. Notice what you see, hear and smell. Research shows even 20 minutes makes a measurable difference to your mood.
actions.impact: Zero carbon and significant wellbeing benefit

actions.title: Invite one other person to join you outdoors
actions.desc: Being in nature is good. Being in nature with someone is better. Suggest an outdoor walk, cycle or park visit to someone you care about this week.

actions.title: Learn about Ireland's saltmarshes and seagrass beds
actions.desc: Go to npws.ie to read about Ireland's coastal habitats. Saltmarshes sit in sheltered bays around Ireland and are some of the most carbon-dense ecosystems in the country. They don't look like much. They are.
actions.impact: Builds awareness of Irish blue carbon ecosystems

actions.title: Choose only certified sustainable seafood this week
actions.desc: Sustainable fishing protects the coastal places that matter most for blue carbon storage, seagrass beds and the habitats beside mangroves. Look for the MSC label.

actions.title: Support WWF's tiger conservation work
actions.desc: Go to wwf.ie to see how tiger conservation works and how your support reaches the field protection teams. Even a small monthly donation pays for habitat protection and anti-poaching work.
actions.impact: Supports habitat protection for endangered species

actions.title: Reflect on what biodiversity means to you and share it with one person
actions.desc: Biodiversity is abstract until it's personal. Think of a wild animal, plant or landscape you love and tell someone why it matters to you. Personal stories move people more than anything else.

actions.title: Use a pocket ashtray instead of dropping the butt
actions.desc: If you smoke or vape, a small tin or pouch ashtray is cheap and stops butts washing into the drains and rivers.
actions.impact: Reduces microplastic and toxin pollution in waterways

actions.title: Pick up 3 cigarette butts next time you're out for a walk
actions.desc: Sounds small, I know. But every butt kept out of a drain is one less source of microplastics and chemicals in the water.
actions.impact: Prevents chemical leaching into local water systems

actions.title: Pick one new habit and attach it to something you already do
actions.desc: Like a reusable cup when you get coffee, or switching devices off before bed. Hook it onto something you do anyway.

actions.title: Do a 10-minute home energy check
actions.desc: Walk around your home and note anything using energy for nothing. Most fixes take minutes. I found more than I expected on my first lap.
actions.impact: Up to 100 kg CO2/year if acted on

actions.title: Learn to identify 3 native hedgerow species near you
actions.desc: Blackthorn, hawthorn and hazel are common in Irish hedges. Start with those three.
actions.impact: Builds awareness of local biodiversity loss

actions.title: Support a local hedgerow or tree planting scheme
actions.desc: One mature hedge can support hundreds of species. Hundreds, from one hedge.
actions.impact: Sequesters roughly 50% more carbon than a similar area of forestry

actions.title: Fix a dripping tap this week
actions.desc: One dripping tap can waste over 5,000 litres of water a year.
actions.impact: Saves thousands of litres of treated water annually

actions.title: Take one minute off your shower
actions.desc: Small change, adds up fast across a household. Go on then.
actions.impact: Can save over 5,000 litres per person per year

actions.title: Report white-tailed eagle sightings if you spot one
actions.desc: Golden Eagle Trust and NPWS track sightings to keep an eye on the population. I'd love to see one.
actions.impact: Supports population monitoring and conservation research

actions.title: Support an elephant or raptor conservation charity
actions.desc: Small, regular donations fund habitat protection and anti-poaching work. Steady beats big and once.
actions.impact: Funds habitat protection for endangered species

actions.title: Plan one Irish trip this year instead of flying
actions.desc: Explore a county you've never been to, by train or car. I'm collecting counties. Slowly.
actions.impact: Avoids the highest-carbon part of most holidays

actions.title: If you do fly, choose direct routes
actions.desc: Layovers mean extra take-offs and landings, the most fuel-heavy part of any flight. I know a thing or two about take-offs.
actions.impact: Cuts unnecessary take-off and landing emissions

actions.title: Check the EPA's bathing water status before you swim
actions.desc: Takes a minute, and you'll know what you're swimming in.
actions.impact: Protects your own health and highlights pollution hotspots

actions.title: Cut back on garden fertiliser this month
actions.desc: Excess nutrients feed the same algae blooms hitting places like Lough Neagh. I saw the photos. Not pretty.

actions.title: Learn what Bord na Móna's rehabilitation programme covers
actions.desc: It's restoring 33,000 hectares of former industrial peatland across 82 midland bogs, over half already done. I'd never seen a bog before I landed.
actions.impact: Supports Ireland's largest peatland carbon restoration programme

actions.title: Visit a restored bog walk near you
actions.desc: Many restored midland bogs now have boardwalks and trails. A good way to see peatland recovery for yourself, and springier than I expected.
actions.impact: Builds public support for peatland restoration

actions.title: Check for a uniform swap or secondhand scheme at school
actions.desc: Lots of parent associations run informal swaps. Worth asking before you buy new.
actions.impact: Extends the useful life of school uniforms

actions.title: Reuse stationery and bags from last year where you can
actions.desc: A schoolbag or pencil case that still works doesn't need replacing just because the year changed.
actions.impact: Reduces demand for new school supplies

actions.title: Check what share of your electricity supplier's mix is renewable
actions.desc: Most Irish suppliers publish a fuel mix disclosure. Worth a look. I was curious what was actually behind the socket.

actions.title: Time energy-heavy tasks for windier days if you can
actions.desc: Ireland's grid runs cleanest when wind output is high, so a small shift in timing helps. Turns out the weather is good for something.
actions.impact: Shifts demand toward cleaner grid periods

actions.title: Use your brown bin for garden and food waste this BBQ season
actions.desc: Grass clippings and food scraps go in there, not the general bin.
actions.impact: Diverts waste from landfill to composting

actions.title: Portion your BBQ food a little more carefully
actions.desc: Cooking too much is one of the most common reasons summer food gets wasted. A rough headcount before you shop helps.
actions.impact: Reduces food waste at the source

actions.title: Join a bat walk this month
actions.desc: Lots of local heritage and biodiversity groups run evening bat walks with bat detectors. I'm going too.
actions.impact: Builds appreciation and awareness of local biodiversity

actions.title: Leave a corner of your garden a little wild
actions.desc: Long grass and native shrubs bring in the insects that bats feed on.
actions.impact: Supports local insect and bat populations

actions.title: Let one patch of your garden or green space grow wild this month
actions.desc: Late summer wildflowers like ivy and heather are a vital late-season food source for bees. The last shift, basically.
actions.impact: Supports pollinator food sources before winter

actions.title: Check if your workplace or community group is on the AIPP list
actions.desc: Businesses, schools and community groups can sign up to take specific pollinator-friendly actions. Is yours on it yet?

actions.title: Try repairing one item before replacing it
actions.desc: A patch, a stitch or a trip to the cobbler often costs far less than buying new. Fair play to the cobbler, I didn't know that job still existed.
actions.impact: Extends the useful life of existing garments

actions.title: Drop unwanted textiles at a collection point, not the general bin
actions.desc: Textile banks and charity shops keep clothes in use instead of landfill.
actions.impact: Diverts textiles from landfill into reuse

actions.title: Learn if your area has a local coastal or flood risk plan
actions.desc: Local authority websites often have flood risk maps. Worth a look if you're near the coast or a river. Better to know.
actions.impact: Builds awareness of local climate risk

actions.title: Support dune and coastal habitat restoration where you can
actions.desc: Healthy dune systems are a natural buffer against erosion and storm surges. The sea here doesn't mess about, so that matters.

actions.title: Check in on elderly or vulnerable neighbours during a heatwave
actions.desc: Heat illness is a real and growing risk, even in Ireland's famously mild summers.

actions.title: Learn your area's wildfire risk if you're near forest or gorse land
actions.desc: Ireland has had its own gorse and forest fires in dry spells. Knowing the risk where you live helps you act early. I didn't expect fires in a place this rainy.

actions.title: Follow research updates from Irish biodiversity conferences
actions.desc: Universities and NPWS often share key findings publicly after events like this. Worth a follow.

actions.title: Share one surprising biodiversity fact with someone this week
actions.desc: Awareness is often the first step towards support for conservation funding and policy. Pick the one that surprised you most.
actions.impact: Builds broader public support for conservation

actions.title: Do a wardrobe audit this weekend
actions.desc: Count how many things you haven't worn in a year. That's your list of what to sell, swap or donate.
actions.impact: Highlights overconsumption without needing a purchase

actions.title: Look up your nearest clothes swap or charity shop
actions.desc: Ireland has a serious charity shop culture, I noticed that early on. Check what's already out there before buying new.
actions.impact: Extends the useful life of existing garments

actions.title: Take the Second-Hand September pledge
actions.desc: Buy nothing new this month. Try a charity shop, a swap or an online secondhand marketplace first. I'm giving it a go myself.
actions.impact: Avoids emissions from new garment production

actions.title: Sell or donate 5 items you no longer wear
actions.desc: Someone else's secondhand find starts in your wardrobe.
actions.impact: Extends the useful life of existing garments

actions.title: Try one organic swap in your weekly shop
actions.desc: Pick one thing, maybe your fruit and veg, and go organic for a week.

actions.title: Look for the EU organic logo when shopping
actions.desc: The green leaf logo means the product meets strict EU organic farming standards. Easy to spot once you know it.
actions.impact: Helps identify verified organic produce quickly

actions.title: Walk or cycle the school run at least once this week
actions.desc: Even one day makes a difference to the traffic and the air outside the school gates.
actions.impact: Cuts short-trip car emissions near schools

actions.title: Check if there's a Safe Routes scheme near your school
actions.desc: See what's planned or already built near you, and back it if there's a local consultation on.

actions.title: Check your attic and wall insulation
actions.desc: Poor insulation is one of the biggest reasons Irish homes lose heat. SEAI grants can cover a large share of the upgrade cost. I felt the draught before I read the data.
actions.impact: Cuts heat loss and heating-related emissions

actions.title: Bleed your radiators before the cold sets in
actions.desc: Trapped air makes a radiator work harder for less heat. A five-minute job, and oddly satisfying.

actions.title: Check if smoky coal or turf is legal to burn in your area
actions.desc: The rules have been tightening across Ireland. A quick check saves you breaking them without knowing.

actions.title: Get your solid fuel stove serviced
actions.desc: A stove that isn't looked after burns less efficiently and makes more smoke.

actions.title: Watch for a murmuration at dusk this month
actions.desc: Starlings gather at reliable roost sites just before sunset. BirdWatch Ireland lists the known spots. I want to see one.
actions.impact: Builds appreciation and awareness of local biodiversity

actions.title: Record a wildlife sighting on a citizen science app
actions.desc: Apps like iNaturalist or BirdTrack let you log what you see, and the data genuinely helps researchers. Your sighting, their dataset.
actions.impact: Supports species and seasonal monitoring data

actions.title: Add one seasonal Irish item to your shop this week
actions.desc: Irish apples, blackberries or kale instead of the imported ones. I checked the prices, it's often cheaper too.

actions.title: Check the origin label before you buy fruit and veg
actions.desc: Takes a second, and it builds the habit of noticing where your food comes from.

actions.title: Reach out to check in with someone today
actions.desc: A short message or call to someone you haven't talked to in a while matters more than you think. I'm far from home. I know.

actions.title: Take a 15-minute walk somewhere green
actions.desc: Doesn't need to be long or far. A local park, a riverside path, a bit of coast all count. Even in the rain, which is often.

actions.title: Refuse single-use cutlery or straws this week
actions.desc: Say no when they're offered, or carry a small reusable set. Over hundreds of takeaways a year, it adds up.

actions.title: Do one plastic-free grocery shop
actions.desc: Loose fruit and veg, and packaging-free options where you can find them. Harder than it sounds.

actions.title: Look up what Ireland's carbon tax actually funds
actions.desc: A few minutes on gov.ie shows exactly where the ring-fenced revenue goes. I looked, it's very specific.
actions.impact: Builds understanding of national climate policy

actions.title: Follow COP31 coverage as it happens
actions.desc: Even a few days of proper coverage gives a much clearer picture than headlines alone. I'll be watching too.

actions.title: Learn one action from Ireland's National Biodiversity Action Plan
actions.desc: A few minutes on npws.ie shows practical steps happening at national level. Pick one and see what it actually means on the ground.
actions.impact: Builds understanding of national biodiversity policy

actions.title: Support a local biodiversity project
actions.desc: From community gardens to local Tidy Towns biodiversity projects, small local efforts add up. Fair play to the people running them.
actions.impact: Supports local habitat and species protection

actions.title: Check your fridge and AC unit are properly serviced
actions.desc: Older units can still leak banned refrigerant gases if damaged or not looked after.
actions.impact: Prevents leaks of ozone-depleting and warming gases

actions.title: Learn one thing about an environmental success story
actions.desc: The ozone layer is proof that the world can fix something when it agrees to. I saw the hole from up there. It's closing. Worth telling someone.

actions.title: Swap one short car trip for walking or cycling this week
actions.desc: If it's under 5km, there's a good chance you could walk or cycle it just as easily. Go on then.

actions.title: Check out Climate Carnival or a local Mobility Week event near you
actions.desc: Local events often have free bike checks, taster cycling sessions or public transport demos. Go on, have a look.
actions.impact: Builds engagement with local low-carbon transport options

actions.title: Try one bamboo product swap
actions.desc: Toothbrushes, socks and kitchen utensils are the usual starting points. Watch out for bamboo viscose fabric though. It's heavily processed and loses much of the benefit.

actions.title: Look for FSC or verified sourcing on bamboo products
actions.desc: Not all bamboo is grown or processed responsibly. A recognised certification is the simple way to check.

actions.title: Support Irish Aid or a climate justice charity
actions.desc: Groups like Trócaire work directly with the communities facing the worst of it.
actions.impact: Supports climate adaptation in vulnerable regions

actions.title: Leave the car home for one trip today
actions.desc: Walk, cycle or bus one journey you'd normally drive. I'm doing the same today.
actions.impact: Cuts one day's worth of car emissions

actions.title: Check your local Local Link or bus route
actions.desc: Many areas have more options than people realise. Turns out there was a bus near me all along.
actions.impact: Builds awareness of low-carbon transport options

actions.title: Try a Leap Card or local transport app for a week
actions.desc: See how far one card or app gets you across buses, trains and trams. A week is long enough to find out.

actions.title: Cycle or walk one journey you'd usually drive
actions.desc: Doesn't need to be your commute. A short errand counts.

actions.title: Suggest a green idea at work this week
actions.desc: A bike rack, a recycling audit. Small changes that lift morale too. Fair play for asking.

actions.title: Try one active or public transport commute this week
actions.desc: Even once counts. Once is grand.

actions.title: Check mywaste.ie for anything you're unsure about
actions.desc: Two minutes now saves a contaminated bin later. I check it more than I'd like to admit.

actions.title: Make sure recycling is clean, dry and loose
actions.desc: Food left on things, and recycling put in bags, are the usual reasons a batch gets rejected. Clean and loose, that's it.

actions.title: Start a bottle jar at home
actions.desc: A few euro in deposits adds up fast, and none of it ends up as litter. Grand little system.
actions.impact: Diverts containers from landfill into the return stream

actions.title: Find your nearest Re-Turn point
actions.desc: Most supermarkets have a machine, many corner shops take returns over the counter. Grand once you know where.

actions.title: Plan your meals before you shop this week
actions.desc: A rough list stops food going off before you get round to it.

actions.title: Start composting food waste if you don't already
actions.desc: Composting cuts food waste's climate impact by more than 90% versus landfill. That surprised me.
actions.impact: Cuts methane emissions from landfilled food waste

actions.title: Choose products with less packaging, not just recyclable packaging
actions.desc: Less packaging beats recyclable packaging every time. Took me a while to get that one.
actions.impact: Cuts packaging waste at the source

actions.title: Rinse and dry your recycling before it goes out
actions.desc: A few seconds under the tap stops a whole batch getting contaminated. Cheap insurance.

actions.title: Switch to a certified sustainable coffee brand
actions.desc: Next time you buy beans or ground coffee, look for Rainforest Alliance or organic certification on the bag.
actions.impact: Reduces water use and land pressure per kg of beans

actions.title: Replace one car journey with public transport this week
actions.desc: One return trip by bus or train instead of the car, done weekly, saves roughly 50 kg CO₂ over the year. I checked the sum twice.
actions.impact: ~50 kg CO₂ saved/year if done weekly

actions.title: Try one lamb-free week this month
actions.desc: Lamb has one of the biggest footprints of any meat. Swapping it for chicken or legumes makes a real difference.
actions.impact: ~28 kg CO₂ saved per kg avoided

actions.title: Buy your next pair of shoes second-hand or from a sustainable brand
actions.desc: Making one pair of leather shoes produces ~30 kg CO₂. Second-hand or vegan options cut that dramatically.
actions.impact: Up to 30 kg CO₂ saved per pair

actions.title: Try one beef-free week
actions.desc: Beef is the highest-impact everyday food I've come across. Swap it for chicken, fish or plant protein just once a week and it adds up.
actions.impact: ~60 kg CO₂ saved per kg avoided

actions.title: Keep your current phone for one more year
actions.desc: Making a new smartphone produces ~70 kg CO₂. The best phone for the planet is the one already in your pocket.

actions.title: Buy your next bike second-hand
actions.desc: Making a new bicycle uses ~96 kg CO₂. Second-hand cuts that to near zero, and saves you money too.

actions.title: Choose a local or low-travel event for your next big trip
actions.desc: One trip to a big sporting event can cost 125 kg CO₂. Picking one within driving distance makes a big difference. I ran the numbers twice.
actions.impact: ~125 kg CO₂ saved per trip avoided

actions.title: Repair or refurbish your laptop instead of buying new
actions.desc: A new laptop produces ~300 kg CO₂ in manufacturing alone. Most repairs cost a fraction of that and give it years more. Mine's been patched more than once.

actions.title: Replace one short-haul flight with a train or ferry
actions.desc: A return Dublin to Madrid flight makes about 550 kg CO₂. For trips under 5 to 6 hours the train usually works, and it's far lower impact.

actions.title: Enable downloads instead of streaming this week
actions.desc: Streaming keeps data centres busy the whole time. Download music or videos on Wi-Fi and watch offline, and that energy use drops a good bit.
actions.impact: Part of your ~636 kg/year digital footprint

actions.title: Switch your dog to a lower-impact food brand
actions.desc: A dog's footprint is about 770 kg CO₂ a year, mostly from meat-based food. A few brands now do lower-carbon recipes with insect or plant protein. The dog won't mind.

actions.title: Plan your meals this week to reduce food waste
actions.desc: The average household throws away enough food to make 1,600 kg CO₂ a year. A simple weekly plan and a look in the fridge before shopping can cut that in half.

actions.title: Swap one beef meal a week for chicken, or for beans and lentils
actions.desc: A 200 g beef portion is 3,083 L of water. The same portion of chicken is 865 L. That's the biggest single lever in the whole dataset. One meal, not your whole diet.

actions.title: Eat what you buy: finish the cheese, bread and leftovers in time
actions.desc: Waste a 1 kg block of cheese and 3,178 L go with it. An 800 g loaf, 1,286 L. Food you already own is the cheapest water saving there is.
actions.impact: 3,178 L per wasted kilo of cheese

actions.title: Get one more year out of the clothes you own before replacing them
actions.desc: One t-shirt is 2,495 L, one pair of jeans is 8,000 L. Not buying one garment beats months of shorter showers. That one surprised me.

actions.title: Turn the tap off while you brush
actions.desc: 12 L becomes 1 L, twice a day. Costs nothing, and over a year it's about three t-shirts' worth of water.

actions.title: Take two minutes off your shower
actions.desc: A standard showerhead runs at 9 L a minute. Same sort of size as the toothbrush habit. Small, but it compounds, every single day.

actions.title: Fix the tap that drips
actions.desc: A slow drip is about 15 L a day. A ten-minute job that keeps paying off for the rest of the year.
